nodes.name: $k$-vector
nodes.statement: As alluded to above, just as linear algebra is the natural language of "little arrows," exterior algebra is the natural language of "little volumes" which we will call $k$-vectors.

nodes.name: 2-vector $u \wedge v$
nodes.statement: As a shorthand, we will denote this little parallelogram or 2-vector as $u \wedge v$ (here the $\wedge$ symbol is pronounced "wedge").

nodes.name: 3-vector $u \wedge v \wedge w$
nodes.statement: Just as with 2-vectors, we can denote this little volume or 3-vector as $u \wedge v \wedge w$.

nodes.name: Permutations and orientation of 3-vectors
nodes.statement: By playing around a bit more we can notice that every time we swap a pair of consecutive vectors in a 3-vector the orientation switches; if we swap another pair the orientation switches back. Hence, any even permutation of vectors preserves orientation; any odd permutation reverses orientation.
conclusions: any even permutation of vectors preserves orientation; any odd permutation reverses orientation

nodes.name: Wedge product (rules)
nodes.statement: Already we've established a bunch of rules about how little volumes appear to behave, which start to provide a definition for the wedge product $\wedge$. In particular, for any collection of vectors $u, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and scalars $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ we have \begin{itemize} \item[-] (Antisymmetry) $u \wedge v=-v \wedge u$ \item[-] (Associativity) $(u \wedge v) \wedge w=u \wedge(v \wedge w)$ \item[-] (Distributivity over addition) $u \wedge(v+w)=u \wedge v+u \wedge w$ \item[-] (Distributivity of scalar multiplication) $(a u) \wedge(b v)=a b(u \wedge v)$ \end{itemize} In fact, these rules provide the right impression of how the wedge product behaves in any vector space, for any number of vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Wedge product on vectors: antisymmetric, associative, distributive over addition, bilinear in scalars.

nodes.name: Hodge star on $k$-vectors
nodes.statement: In exterior algebra, the Hodge star ★ (pronounced "star") provides a sort of orthogonal complement for $k$-vectors. In particular, if we have a $k$-vector $v$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, then $\star v$ will be an $(n-k)$-vector that is in some sense "complementary."

nodes.name: Hodge star of a 2-vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$
nodes.statement: For a 2-vector $u \wedge v$, we'll ask that $$ \operatorname{det}(u, v, \star(u \wedge v))>0, $$ i.e., the determinant of the two vectors comprising $u \wedge v$ and the third vector given by its Hodge star should be positive. In fact, this rule corresponds to the usual right-hand rule in the sense that ★ $(u \wedge v)$ points in the same direction as $u \times v$. What about the magnitude? Again we have a rule based on the determinant-in particular, in the special case of two orthonormal vectors $u_{1}, u_{2}$, we ask that $$ \operatorname{det}\left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \star\left(u_{1} \wedge u_{2}\right)\right)=1 . $$
nodes.statement_short: Orientation of star(u∧v) fixed by positive determinant; magnitude by det=1 for orthonormal u1,u2.

nodes.name: Justification of $\star(u\wedge v)=u\times v$
nodes.statement: Since vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ can always be expressed in an orthonormal basis, this rule uniquely pins down the Hodge star for any 2-vector.
nodes.statement_short: Expand in an orthonormal basis; the determinant rule fixes the star uniquely.

nodes.name: $\star(u\wedge v)=u\times v$
nodes.statement: In particular, we now really have $\star(u \wedge v)=u \times v$, i.e., for two vectors in Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ applying the wedge and then the star is equivalent to taking the cross product. (But it will not be this easy in general!)

nodes.name: Hodge star via orthonormal $k$-vectors
nodes.statement: More generally, suppose $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{n}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. If we start out with $k$ orthonormal vectors $u_{1}, \ldots, u_{k}$, then the Hodge star is uniquely determined by the relationship $$ \left(u_{1} \wedge \cdots \wedge u_{k}\right) \wedge \star\left(u_{1} \wedge \cdots \wedge u_{k}\right)=e_{1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{n} . $$
nodes.statement_short: Star of a unit k-vector is the complementary unit (n-k)-vector whose wedge with it is e1∧...∧en.

nodes.name: 2D Hodge star is a quarter rotation
nodes.statement: In other words, in 2D the Hodge star is just a quarter-rotation in the counter-clockwise direction.
conclusions: the Hodge star is just a quarter-rotation in the counter-clockwise direction

nodes.name: Hodge star distributes over addition
nodes.statement: For instance, for two 1-vectors $u, v$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, we have $$ \star(u+v)=\star u+\star v, $$ since adding two vectors and then rotating them by 90 degrees is no different from rotating them each individually and then adding them. More generally, this same identity holds for any two $k$-vectors in any dimension, i.e., the Hodge star distributes over addition (can you draw other pictures that make this idea clearer?).
conclusions: the Hodge star distributes over addition

nodes.name: Example 1: wedge of two 1-vectors
nodes.statement: EXAMPLE 1. Let $u:=e_{1}+2 e_{2}$ and $v:=e_{1}+e_{2}-e_{3}$ be 1-vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. Then their wedge product is given by $$ \begin{aligned} u \wedge v & =\left(e_{1}+2 e_{2}\right) \wedge\left(e_{1}+e_{2}-e_{3}\right) \\ & =e_{1} \wedge\left(e_{1}+e_{2}-e_{3}\right)+2 e_{2} \wedge\left(e_{1}+e_{2}-e_{3}\right) \\ & =e_{1} \wedge e_{1}+0 e_{1} \wedge e_{2}-e_{1} \wedge e_{3}+2 e_{2} \wedge e_{1}+2 e_{2} \wedge e_{2}-0 \\ & =e_{1} \wedge e_{2}-2 e_{2} \wedge e_{3} \\ & =-e_{1} \wedge e_{2}-e_{1} \wedge e_{3}-2 e_{2} \wedge e_{3} . \end{aligned} $$ There are a couple things to notice in this calculation. First, any term $e_{i} \wedge e_{i}$ cancels to zero. Do you remember why? It's essentially because the parallelogram spanned by two copies of the same vector has zero area. Also notice that at one point we replace $2 e_{2} \wedge e_{1}$ with $-2 e_{1} \wedge e_{2}$. Why did we do that? Because $e_{1} \wedge e_{2}$ and $e_{2} \wedge e_{1}$ describe the same 2-vector, but with opposite orientation.
nodes.section: 4.2. Examples of Wedge and Star in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
nodes.statement_short: Expand (e1+2e2)∧(e1+e2-e3) using antisymmetry and e_i∧e_i=0.

nodes.name: Example 2: Hodge star of a 2-vector
nodes.statement: EXAMPLE 2. Let $w:=-e_{1} \wedge e_{2}-e_{1} \wedge e_{3}-2 e_{2} \wedge e_{3}$ be the 2-vector from the previous example. Its Hodge star is given by $$ \begin{aligned} \star w & =\star\left(-e_{1} \wedge e_{2}-e_{1} \wedge e_{3}-2 e_{2} \wedge e_{3}\right) \\ & =-\star\left(e_{1} \wedge e_{2}\right)-\star\left(e_{1} \wedge e_{3}\right)-2 \star\left(e_{2} \wedge e_{3}\right) \\ & =-e_{3}-\left(-e_{2}\right)-2 e_{1} \\ & =-2 e_{1}+e_{2}-e_{3} . \end{aligned} $$ The main thing we did here was use the right hand rule to determine which direction the wedge of two basis vectors points. For instance, just as $e_{1} \times e_{2}=e_{3}$ when working with the cross product, $\star\left(e_{1} \wedge e_{2}\right)=e_{3}$ when working with the wedge product and the Hodge star. A more detailed discussion of these relationships, and about bases in exterior algebra, can be found in Section 4.5.1.
nodes.section: 4.2. Examples of Wedge and Star in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
nodes.statement_short: Star of a 2-vector in R^3 via the right-hand rule on basis 2-vectors.

nodes.name: Example 3: triple wedge vanishing
nodes.statement: EXAMPLE 3. Let $u:=e_{1}+e_{2}+e_{3}, v:=e_{1}+2 e_{2}+3 e_{3}$, and $w:=e_{1}-e_{3}$ be 1-vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, and suppose we want to compute $u \wedge v \wedge w$. Since the wedge product is associative, we can start out by just computing either $u \wedge v$ or $v \wedge w$, and then wedging the result with the remaining 1-vector. For instance, we have $$ \begin{aligned} v \wedge w & =\left(e_{1}+2 e_{2}+3 e_{3}\right) \wedge\left(e_{1}-e_{3}\right) \\ & =e_{1} \wedge e_{1} \stackrel{\circ}{0} e_{1} \wedge e_{3}+2 e_{2} \wedge e_{1}-2 e_{2} \wedge e_{3}+3 e_{3} \wedge e_{1}-3 e_{3} \wedge e_{3} 0 \\ & =-2 e_{1} \wedge e_{2}-4 e_{1} \wedge e_{3}-2 e_{2} \wedge e_{3} . \end{aligned} $$ Wedging with $u$ then yields $$ \begin{aligned} u \wedge(v \wedge w) & =\left(e_{1}+e_{2}+e_{3}\right) \wedge\left(-2 e_{1} \wedge e_{2}-4 e_{1} \wedge e_{3}-2 e_{2} \wedge e_{3}\right) \\ & =-2 e_{1} \wedge e_{2} \wedge e_{3}-4 e_{2} \wedge e_{1} \wedge e_{3}-2 e_{3} \wedge e_{1} \wedge e_{2} \\ & =-2 e_{1} \wedge e_{2} \wedge e_{3}+4 e_{1} \wedge e_{2} \wedge e_{3}-2 e_{1} \wedge e_{2} \wedge e_{3} \\ & =0 . \end{aligned} $$ In the second calculation we avoided a lot of work by noticing that any term involving multiple copies of the same basis 1-vector (e.g., $e_{1} \wedge e_{1} \wedge e_{2}$ ) would have zero volume, since two of the edges of the corresponding little parallelepiped would be parallel. Hence, we can just write down the three remaining terms where all three bases show up (e.g., $e_{2} \wedge e_{3} \wedge e_{1}$ ). By repeatedly swapping pairs of bases, we can put all such 3-vectors into a canonical form (e.g., $e_{2} \wedge e_{3} \wedge e_{1}=-e_{2} \wedge e_{1} \wedge e_{3}=$ $e_{1} \wedge e_{2} \wedge e_{3}$ ), at which point we just have several copies of the unit 3-vector $e_{1} \wedge e_{2} \wedge e_{3}$ scaled by some magnitude. In this case, the magnitudes of all the terms summed to zero. What does that mean geometrically? It must mean that our original 1-vectors $u, v$, and $w$ are not linearly independent, i.e., they describe a "flat" 3-vector with zero volume.
nodes.section: 4.2. Examples of Wedge and Star in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
nodes.statement_short: u∧v∧w computed by associativity is zero, so u, v, w are linearly dependent.

nodes.name: 1-form (covector)
nodes.statement: The notation here is meant to emphasize the idea that $\alpha$ is a function: in particular, it's a linear function that eats a vector and produces a scalar. Any such function is called a 1-form (also known as a covector).
differentia: eats a vector and produces a scalar

nodes.name: Sharp and flat
nodes.statement: Same deal with vectors and 1-forms, except that now we have two different operations: sharp $(\sharp)$, which converts a 1-form into a vector, and flat (b) which converts a vector into a 1-form.

nodes.name: Musical isomorphisms
nodes.statement: The operations \# and b are called the musical isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Surface map $f$
nodes.statement: It's important to remember that tangent vectors get stretched out by the map $f: \mathbb{R}^{2} \supset M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{3}$ that takes us from the plane to some surface in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$.

nodes.name: Induced metric $g$
nodes.statement: Therefore, the operations $\sharp$ and $b$ should satisfy relationships like $$ u^{b}(v)=g(u, v) $$ where $g$ is the metric induced by $f$.

nodes.name: Coordinate bases $\partial/\partial x^i$ and $dx^i$
nodes.statement: For reasons that will become clear later, we're going to use the symbols $\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{n}}$ to represent an orthonormal basis for vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, and use $d x^{1}, \ldots, d x^{n}$ to denote the corresponding 1-form basis. In other words, any vector $v$ can be written as a linear combination $$ v=v^{1} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}+\cdots+v^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{n}}, $$ and any 1-form can be written as a linear combination $$ \alpha=\alpha_{1} d x^{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{n} d x^{n} . $$

nodes.name: Dual bases
nodes.statement: The two bases $d x^{i}$ and $\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i}}$ are often referred to as dual bases, meaning they satisfy the relationship $$ d x^{i}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\right)=\delta_{j}^{i}= \begin{cases}1, & i=j \\ 0, & \text { otherwise } .\end{cases} $$

nodes.name: Pairing of 1-form and vector
nodes.statement: Using this relationship, we can work out that $$ \alpha(v)=\sum_{i} \alpha_{i} d x^{i}\left(\sum_{j} v^{j} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{j}}\right)=\sum_{i} \alpha_{i} v^{i} $$ i.e., the pairing of a vector and a 1-form looks just like the standard Euclidean inner product.

nodes.name: Einstein summation notation
nodes.statement: The reason for being so neurotic is to take advantage of Einstein summation notation: any time a pair of variables is indexed by the same letter $i$ in both the "up" and "down" position, we interpret this as a sum over all possible values of $i$ : $$ \alpha_{i} v^{i}=\sum_{i} \alpha_{i} v^{i} . $$

nodes.name: Sharp raises indices
nodes.statement: Therefore, to go from a 1-form to a vector we raise the indices. For instance, in a flat space we don't have to worry about the metric and so a 1 -form $$ \alpha=\alpha_{1} d x^{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{n} d x^{n} $$ becomes a vector $$ \alpha^{\sharp}=\alpha^{1} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}+\cdots+\alpha^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{n}} . $$

nodes.name: Flat lowers indices
nodes.statement: Similarly, $b$ indicates a decrease in pitch and a downward motion on the staff: \footnotetext{${ }^{3}$ At least on a tempered instrument! } \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{5ca462c8-87f1-4b78-bcfe-c2b572a4db96-35_133_220_253_950}\\ and so $b$ lowers the indices of a vector to give us a 1-form-e.g., $$ v=v^{1} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}+\cdots+v^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{n}} . $$ becomes $$ v^{b}=v_{1} d x^{1}+\cdots+v_{n} d x^{n} . $$

nodes.name: Wedge of two 1-forms
nodes.statement: Since we want to measure a lot of projected volumes in the future, we'll give this operation the special name " $\alpha \wedge \beta^{\prime \prime}$ : $$ \alpha \wedge \beta(u, v):=\alpha(u) \beta(v)-\alpha(v) \beta(u) . $$
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: 2-form
nodes.statement: As you may have already guessed, $\alpha \wedge \beta$ is what we call a 2-form.
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Antisymmetry of the wedge of 1-forms
nodes.statement: For instance, notice that if we reverse the order of our axes $\alpha, \beta$ the sign of the area changes. In other words, the wedge product is antisymmetric: $$ \alpha \wedge \beta=-\beta \wedge \alpha . $$
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Wedge of a 1-form with itself is zero
nodes.statement: An important consequence of antisymmetry is that the wedge of any 1-form with itself is zero: $$ \begin{aligned} & \alpha \wedge \alpha=-\alpha \wedge \alpha \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha \wedge \alpha=0 . \end{aligned} $$
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product
conclusions: the wedge of any 1-form with itself is zero

nodes.name: Wedge distributes over addition
nodes.statement: Next, consider the projection onto two different planes spanned by $\alpha, \beta$ and $\alpha, \gamma$. The sum of the projected areas can be written as $$ \begin{aligned} \alpha \wedge \beta(u, v)+\alpha \wedge \gamma(u, v) & =\alpha(u) \beta(v)-\alpha(v) \beta(u)+\alpha(u) \gamma(v)-\alpha(v) \gamma(u) \\ & =\alpha(u)(\beta(v)+\gamma(v))-\alpha(v)(\beta(u)+\gamma(u)) \\ & =(\alpha \wedge(\beta+\gamma))(u, v), \end{aligned} $$ or in other words $\wedge$ distributes over + : $$ \alpha \wedge(\beta+\gamma)=\alpha \wedge \beta+\alpha \wedge \gamma . $$
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Wedge of three 1-forms (determinant)
nodes.statement: One way to write the projected volume is as the determinant of the projected vectors $u^{\prime}, v^{\prime}$, and $w^{\prime}$ : $$ \alpha \wedge \beta \wedge \gamma(u, v, w):=\operatorname{det}\left(\left[\begin{array}{lll} u^{\prime} & v^{\prime} & w^{\prime} \end{array}\right]\right)=\operatorname{det}\left(\left[\begin{array}{lll} \alpha(u) & \alpha(v) & \alpha(w) \\ \beta(u) & \beta(v) & \beta(w) \\ \gamma(u) & \gamma(v) & \gamma(w) \end{array}\right]\right) . $$
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Triple-product argument for associativity
nodes.statement: Thinking about things this way, we might come up with an alternative definition of the wedge product in terms of the triple product: $$ \begin{aligned} \alpha \wedge \beta \wedge \gamma(u, v, w) & =\left(u^{\prime} \times v^{\prime}\right) \cdot w^{\prime} \\ & =\left(v^{\prime} \times w^{\prime}\right) \cdot u^{\prime} \\ & =\left(w^{\prime} \times u^{\prime}\right) \cdot v^{\prime} \end{aligned} $$ The important thing to notice here is that order is not important-we always get the same volume, regardless of which face we pick (though we still have to be a bit careful about sign).
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product
nodes.statement_short: Volume as face area times edge length is independent of the face chosen.

nodes.name: Associativity of the wedge of 1-forms
nodes.statement: A more algebraic way of saying this is that the wedge product is associative: $$ (\alpha \wedge \beta) \wedge \gamma=\alpha \wedge(\beta \wedge \gamma) . $$
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Properties of the wedge product of forms
nodes.statement: In summary, the wedge product of $k 1$-forms gives us a $k$-form, which measures the projected volume of a collection of $k$ vectors. As a result, the wedge product has the following properties for any $k$-form $\alpha, l$-form $\beta$, and $m$-form $\gamma$ : \begin{itemize} \item[-] Antisymmetry: $\alpha \wedge \beta=(-1)^{k l} \beta \wedge \alpha$ \item[-] Associativity: $\alpha \wedge(\beta \wedge \gamma)=(\alpha \wedge \beta) \wedge \gamma$ \end{itemize} and in the case where $\beta$ and $\gamma$ have the same degree (i.e., $l=m$ ) we have \begin{itemize} \item[-] Distributivity: $\alpha \wedge(\beta+\gamma)=\alpha \wedge \beta+\alpha \wedge \gamma$ \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product
assumptions: in the case where $\beta$ and $\gamma$ have the same degree (i.e., $l=m$ )
in the case where $\beta$ and $\gamma$ have the same degree (i.e., $l=m$ )

nodes.statement_short: Wedge of forms: graded antisymmetry (-1)^{kl}, associativity, and distributivity over same-degree sums.

nodes.name: $k$-forms are antisymmetric in their arguments
nodes.statement: A separate fact is that a $k$-form is antisymmetric in its arguments-in other words, swapping the relative order of two "input" vectors changes only the sign of the volume. For instance, if $\alpha$ is a 2-form then $\alpha(u, v)=-\alpha(v, u)$. In general, an even number of swaps will preserve the sign; an odd number of swaps will negate it.
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Multilinear
nodes.statement: Finally, you'll often hear people say that $k$-forms are "multilinear"-all this means is that if you keep all but one of the vectors fixed, then a $k$-form looks like a linear map.
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Surface map as vector-valued forms
nodes.statement: A good example of a vector-valued $k$-form is our map $f: M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{3}$ which represents the geometry of a surface. In the language of exterior calculus, $f$ is an $\mathbb{R}^{3}$-valued 0 -form: at each point $p$ of $M$, it takes zero vectors as input and produces a point $f(p)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ as output. Similarly, the differential $d f$ is an $\mathbb{R}^{3}$-valued 1-form: it takes one vector (some direction $u$ in the plane) and maps it to a value $d f(u)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ (representing the "stretched out" version of $u$ ).
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: $E$-valued $k$-form
nodes.statement: More generally, if $E$ is a vector space then an $E$-valued $k$-form takes $k$ vectors to a single value in $E$.
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: $\mathbb{R}^3$-valued 2-form via cross product
nodes.statement: In other cases we simply have to say which product we want to use-in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ for instance we could use the cross product ×, in which case an $\mathbb{R}^{3}$-valued 2-form looks like this: $$ \alpha \wedge \beta(u, v):=\alpha(u) \times \beta(v)-\alpha(v) \times \beta(u) . $$
nodes.section: 4.4. Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

nodes.name: Idea of Hodge duality
nodes.statement: This observation captures the idea behind Hodge duality: a $k$-dimensional volume in an $n$-dimensional space can be specified either by $k$ directions or by a complementary set of $(n-k)$ directions.

nodes.name: Constant 0-form 1
nodes.statement: 0-forms are easy: any 0-form can be thought of as some function times the constant 0-form, which we'll denote "1."

nodes.name: Complete list of $k$-form bases on $\mathbb{R}^3$
nodes.statement: The complete list of $k$-form bases on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is then \begin{itemize} \item[-] 0-form bases: 1 \item[-] 1-form bases: $d x^{1}, d x^{2}, d x^{3}$ \item[-] 2-form bases: $d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}, d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}, d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}$ \item[-] 3-form bases: $d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}$, \end{itemize} which means the number of bases is 1, 3, 3, 1.

nodes.name: Number of $k$-form bases is $\binom{n}{k}$
nodes.statement: In fact you may see a more general pattern here: the number of $k$-form bases on an $n$-dimensional space is given by the binomial coefficient $$ \binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} $$ (i.e., " $n$ choose $k^{\prime \prime}$ ), since we want to pick $k$ distinct 1 -form bases and don't care about the order.
conclusions: the number of $k$-form bases on an $n$-dimensional space is given by the binomial coefficient

nodes.name: $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n}{n-k}$ gives $k$/$(n-k)$ correspondence
nodes.statement: An important identity here is $$ \binom{n}{k}=\binom{n}{n-k}, $$ which, as anticipated, means that we have a one-to-one relationship between $k$-forms and $(n-k)$ - forms.

nodes.name: Hodge star on differential forms in $\mathbb{R}^3$
nodes.statement: In particular, we can identify any $k$-form with its complement. For example, on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ we have $$ \begin{aligned} \star 1 & =d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3} \\ \star d x^{1} & =d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3} \\ \star d x^{2} & =d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1} \\ \star d x^{3} & =d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \\ \star\left(d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}\right) & =d x^{3} \\ \star\left(d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}\right) & =d x^{1} \\ \star\left(d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}\right) & =d x^{2} \\ \star\left(d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}\right) & =1 \end{aligned} $$ The map ★ (pronounced "star") is called the Hodge star and captures this idea that planes can be identified with their normals and so forth.

nodes.name: Hodge star on a flat space
nodes.statement: More generally, on any flat space we have $$ \star\left(d x^{i_{1}} \wedge d x^{i_{2}} \wedge \cdots \wedge d x^{i_{k}}\right)=d x^{i_{k+1}} \wedge d x^{i_{k+2}} \wedge \cdots \wedge d x^{i_{n}}, $$ where $\left(i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots, i_{n}\right)$ is any even permutation of $(1,2, \ldots, n)$.

nodes.name: Exercise 4.1
nodes.statement: Exercise 4.1\\ Letting $u, v \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ be orthonormal (as above), show that $$ |d f(u) \times d f(v)|=\sqrt{\operatorname{det}(g)}, $$ i.e., show that the "stretching factor" as we go from the plane to the surface is given by the square root of the determinant of the metric $$ \operatorname{det}(g):=g(u, u) g(v, v)-g(u, v)^{2} . $$ Hint: remember that the induced metric is just the usual Fuclidean dot product of the embedded vectors: $g(u, v):=d f(u) \cdot d f(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the area stretching factor |df(u)×df(v)| equals sqrt(det g).

nodes.name: Volume form
nodes.statement: More generally, the $n$-form $$ \omega:=\sqrt{\operatorname{det}(g)} d x^{1} \wedge \cdots \wedge d x^{n} $$ is called the volume form, and will play a key role when we talk about integration.

nodes.name: $\star 1=\omega$ on curved spaces
nodes.statement: For instance, it makes a certain amount of sense to identify the constant function 1 with the volume form $\omega$, since $\omega$ really represents unit volume on the curved space: $$ \star 1=\omega $$

nodes.name: Inner product on $k$-forms
nodes.statement: More generally we'll ask that any $n$-form constructed from a pair of $k$-forms $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfies $$ \alpha \wedge \star \beta=\langle\langle\alpha, \beta\rangle\rangle \omega, $$ where $\langle\langle\alpha, \beta\rangle\rangle=\sum_{i} \alpha_{i} \beta_{i}$ is the inner product on $k$-forms.

nodes.name: Euclidean inner product via wedge and star
nodes.statement: For instance, if $u$ and $v$ are vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, then we can write $$ u \cdot v=\star\left(u^{b} \wedge \star v^{b}\right), $$ i.e., on a flat space we can express the usual Euclidean inner product via the wedge product.

nodes.name: Cross product via wedge and star
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can express the Euclidean cross product as just $$ u \times v=\left(\star\left(u^{b} \wedge v^{b}\right)\right)^{\sharp}, $$ i.e., we can create a plane with normal $u \times v$ by wedging together the two basis vectors $u$ and $v$.

nodes.name: Exterior derivative
nodes.statement: More generally $d$ is called the exterior derivative and is responsible for building up many of the differential operators in exterior calculus.

nodes.name: Nabla operator
nodes.statement: The key player here is the operator ∇ (pronounced "nabla") which can be expressed in coordinates as the vector of all partial derivatives: $$ \nabla:=\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{n}}\right)^{T} . $$

nodes.name: Gradient
nodes.statement: For instance, applying ∇ to a scalar function $\phi: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ yields the gradient $$ \nabla \phi=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^{1}}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^{n}}\right)^{T}, $$ which can be visualized as the direction of steepest ascent on some terrain:

nodes.name: Divergence and curl
nodes.statement: We can also apply ∇ to a vector field $X$ in two different ways. The dot product gives us the divergence $$ \nabla \cdot X=\frac{\partial X^{1}}{\partial x^{1}}+\cdots+\frac{\partial X^{n}}{\partial x^{n}} $$ which measures how quickly the vector field is "spreading out", and on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ the cross product gives us the curl $$ \nabla \times X=\left(\frac{\partial X^{3}}{\partial x^{2}}-\frac{\partial X^{2}}{\partial x^{3}}, \frac{\partial X^{1}}{\partial x^{3}}-\frac{\partial X^{3}}{\partial x^{1}}, \frac{\partial X^{2}}{\partial x^{1}}-\frac{\partial X^{1}}{\partial x^{2}}\right), $$ which indicates how much a vector field is "spinning around."

nodes.name: Differential of a 0-form
nodes.statement: Let's first take a look at the exterior derivative of 0 -forms (i.e., functions), which is often just called the differential. To keep things simple, we'll start with real-valued functions $\phi: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. In coordinates, the differential is defined as $$ d \phi:=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1}+\cdots+\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x^{n}} d x^{n} . $$

nodes.name: $\nabla\phi=(d\phi)^\sharp$
nodes.statement: And indeed the two are closely related, except for the fact that $\nabla \phi$ is a vector field and $d \phi$ is a 1-form. More precisely, $$ \nabla \phi=(d \phi)^{\sharp} . $$

nodes.name: Directional derivative
nodes.statement: In general, $d f(u)$ represents the directional derivative of $f$ along the direction $u$.

nodes.name: $df(u)=u\cdot\nabla f$
nodes.statement: Returning again to vector calculus notation, we have $$ d f(u)=u \cdot \nabla f . $$

nodes.name: Linearity of $d$
nodes.statement: For one thing, we expect $d$ to be linear-after all, a derivative is just the limit of a difference, and differences are certainly linear!

nodes.name: Product rule for the exterior derivative
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\alpha$ is a $k$-form then $d$ obeys the rule $$ d(\alpha \wedge \beta)=d \alpha \wedge \beta+(-1)^{k} \alpha \wedge d \beta . $$

nodes.name: Coordinate derivation of $d\alpha$ as curl
nodes.statement: Applying the linearity of $d$, we have $$ \begin{aligned} d \alpha & =d\left(\alpha_{1} d x^{1}+\alpha_{2} d x^{2}+\alpha_{3} d x^{3}\right) \\ & =d\left(\alpha_{1} d x^{1}\right)+d\left(\alpha_{2} d x^{2}\right)+d\left(\alpha_{3} d x^{3}\right) . \end{aligned} $$ Each term $\alpha_{j} d x^{j}$ can really be thought of a wedge product $\alpha_{j} \wedge d x^{j}$ between a 0 -form $\alpha_{j}$ and the corresponding basis 1-form $d x^{j}$. Applying the exterior derivative to one of these terms we get $$ d\left(\alpha_{j} \wedge d x^{j}\right)=\left(d \alpha_{j}\right) \wedge d x^{j}+\alpha_{j} \wedge \underbrace{\left(d d x^{j}\right)}_{=0}=\frac{\partial \alpha_{j}}{\partial x^{i}} d x^{i} \wedge d x^{j} . $$ To keep things short we used the Einstein summation convention here, but let's really write out all the terms: $$ \begin{aligned} d \alpha= & \frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{1}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{1}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+ \\ & \frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{2}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{2}+ \\ & \frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{3}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{3} . \end{aligned} $$ Using the fact that $\alpha \wedge \beta=-\beta \wedge \alpha$, we get a much simpler expression $$ \begin{aligned} d \alpha= & \left(\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{2}}-\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{3}}\right) d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+ \\ & \left(\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{3}}-\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{1}}\right) d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+ \\ & \left(\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{1}}-\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{2}}\right) d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} . \end{aligned} $$ Does this expression look familiar? If you look again at our review of vector derivatives, you'll recognize that $d \alpha$ basically looks like the curl of $\alpha^{\sharp}$, except that it's expressed as a 2-form instead of a vector field. Also remember (from our discussion of Hodge duality) that a 2-form and a 1-form are not so different here-geometrically they both specify some direction in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand dα in coordinates via linearity and the product rule, then simplify with antisymmetry. The result has the components of the curl as a 2-form.

nodes.name: Apply linearity of d
nodes.statement: Applying the linearity of $d$, we have $$ \begin{aligned} d \alpha & =d\left(\alpha_{1} d x^{1}+\alpha_{2} d x^{2}+\alpha_{3} d x^{3}\right) \\ & =d\left(\alpha_{1} d x^{1}\right)+d\left(\alpha_{2} d x^{2}\right)+d\left(\alpha_{3} d x^{3}\right) . \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Apply linearity of d

nodes.name: Product rule on each term
nodes.statement: Each term $\alpha_{j} d x^{j}$ can really be thought of a wedge product $\alpha_{j} \wedge d x^{j}$ between a 0 -form $\alpha_{j}$ and the corresponding basis 1-form $d x^{j}$. Applying the exterior derivative to one of these terms we get $$ d\left(\alpha_{j} \wedge d x^{j}\right)=\left(d \alpha_{j}\right) \wedge d x^{j}+\alpha_{j} \wedge \underbrace{\left(d d x^{j}\right)}_{=0}=\frac{\partial \alpha_{j}}{\partial x^{i}} d x^{i} \wedge d x^{j} . $$
nodes.statement_short: Product rule on each term

nodes.name: Write out all nine terms
nodes.statement: To keep things short we used the Einstein summation convention here, but let's really write out all the terms: $$ \begin{aligned} d \alpha= & \frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{1}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{1}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+ \\ & \frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{2}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{2}+ \\ & \frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{3}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{3} . \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Write out all nine terms

nodes.name: Simplify by antisymmetry
nodes.statement: Using the fact that $\alpha \wedge \beta=-\beta \wedge \alpha$, we get a much simpler expression $$ \begin{aligned} d \alpha= & \left(\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{2}}-\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{3}}\right) d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+ \\ & \left(\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{3}}-\frac{\partial \alpha_{3}}{\partial x^{1}}\right) d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+ \\ & \left(\frac{\partial \alpha_{2}}{\partial x^{1}}-\frac{\partial \alpha_{1}}{\partial x^{2}}\right) d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} . \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Simplify by antisymmetry

nodes.name: Recognize the curl
nodes.statement: Does this expression look familiar? If you look again at our review of vector derivatives, you'll recognize that $d \alpha$ basically looks like the curl of $\alpha^{\sharp}$, except that it's expressed as a 2-form instead of a vector field. Also remember (from our discussion of Hodge duality) that a 2-form and a 1-form are not so different here-geometrically they both specify some direction in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recognize the curl

nodes.name: Curl via exterior calculus
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can express the curl of any vector field $X$ as $$ \nabla \times X=\left(\star d X^{b}\right)^{\#} . $$

nodes.name: Divergence via exterior calculus
nodes.statement: Therefore, we might suspect that divergence can be computed by first applying the Hodge star, then applying the exterior derivative: $$ \nabla \cdot X=\star d \star X^{b} . $$

nodes.name: Coordinate check of $\nabla\cdot X=\star d\star X^\flat$
nodes.statement: Does this definition really work? Let's give it a try in coordinates on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. First, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \star X^{b} & =\star\left(X_{1} d x^{1}+X_{2} d x^{2}+X_{3} d x^{3}\right) \\ & =X_{1} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+X_{2} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+X_{3} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} . \end{aligned} $$ Differentiating we get $$ \begin{aligned} d \star X^{b}= & \frac{\partial X_{1}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+ \\ & \frac{\partial X_{2}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+ \\ & \frac{\partial X_{3}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}, \end{aligned} $$ but of course we can rearrange these wedge products to simply $$ d \star X^{b}=\left(\frac{\partial X_{1}}{\partial x^{1}}+\frac{\partial X_{2}}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial X_{3}}{\partial x^{3}}\right) d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3} . $$ A final application of the Hodge star gives us the divergence $$ \star d \star X^{b}=\frac{\partial X^{1}}{\partial x^{1}}+\frac{\partial X^{2}}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial X^{3}}{\partial x^{3}} $$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation in R^3 coordinates: star, differentiate, rearrange wedges, star again.

nodes.name: Check in coordinates
nodes.statement: Does this definition really work? Let's give it a try in coordinates on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check in coordinates

nodes.name: Apply the Hodge star to the flat of X
nodes.statement: First, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \star X^{b} & =\star\left(X_{1} d x^{1}+X_{2} d x^{2}+X_{3} d x^{3}\right) \\ & =X_{1} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+X_{2} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+X_{3} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} . \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Hodge star to the flat of X

nodes.name: Differentiate and rearrange
nodes.statement: Differentiating we get $$ \begin{aligned} d \star X^{b}= & \frac{\partial X_{1}}{\partial x^{1}} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3}+ \\ & \frac{\partial X_{2}}{\partial x^{2}} d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1}+ \\ & \frac{\partial X_{3}}{\partial x^{3}} d x^{3} \wedge d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}, \end{aligned} $$ but of course we can rearrange these wedge products to simply $$ d \star X^{b}=\left(\frac{\partial X_{1}}{\partial x^{1}}+\frac{\partial X_{2}}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial X_{3}}{\partial x^{3}}\right) d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} \wedge d x^{3} . $$
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate and rearrange

nodes.name: Final Hodge star gives the divergence
nodes.statement: A final application of the Hodge star gives us the divergence $$ \star d \star X^{b}=\frac{\partial X^{1}}{\partial x^{1}}+\frac{\partial X^{2}}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial X^{3}}{\partial x^{3}} $$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Final Hodge star gives the divergence

nodes.name: Grad, curl and div in exterior calculus
nodes.statement:
In summary, for any scalar field $\phi$ and vector field $X$ we have $$  egin{aligned} 
abla \phi & =(d \phi)^{\sharp} \ 
abla 	imes X & =\left(\star d X^{b}ight)^{\#} \ 
abla \cdot X & =\star d \star X^{b} \end{aligned} $$
assumptions: any scalar field $\phi$ and vector field $X$

nodes.name: Grad, curl, div are $d$ on 0-, 1-, 2-forms
nodes.statement: One cute thing to notice here is that (in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ ) grad, curl, and div are just $d$ applied to a 0-, 1- and 2- form, respectively.

nodes.name: Scalar Laplacian
nodes.statement:
Another key differential operator from vector calculus is the scalar Laplacian which (confusingly!) is often denoted by $\Delta$ or $
abla^{2}$, and is defined as $$ \Delta:=
abla \cdot 
abla, $$ i.e., the divergence of the gradient.

nodes.name: Scalar Laplacian $\Delta=\star d\star d$
nodes.statement: Fortunately, now that we know how to write div, grad and curl using exterior calculus, expressing the scalar Laplacian is straightforward: $\Delta=\star d \star d$.

nodes.name: $k$-form Laplacian
nodes.statement: More generally, the $k$-form Laplacian is given by $$ \Delta:=\star d \star d+d \star d \star . $$

nodes.name: Codifferential
nodes.statement: Some people like to define the operator $\delta:=\star d \star$, called the codifferential, and write the Laplacian as $\Delta=\delta d+d \delta$.

nodes.name: Scalar Laplacian as a special case
nodes.statement: One question you might ask is: why is the Laplacian for 0-forms different from the general $k$-form Laplacian? Actually, it's not-consider what happens when we apply the term $d \star d \star$ to a 0 -form $\phi: \star \phi$ is an $n$-form, and so $d \star \phi$ must be an $(n+1)$-form. But there are no $(n+1)$-forms on an $n$-dimensional space! So this term is often omitted when writing the scalar Laplacian.
nodes.statement_short: On 0-forms the term d★d★ maps into (n+1)-forms, which vanish, so the k-form Laplacian reduces to ★d★d.

nodes.name: Area element is the volume form
nodes.statement: Alternatively, we could write the individual areas using differential forms-in particular, $A_{i}=$ $d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}(u, v)$. Therefore, the area element $d A$ is really nothing more than the standard volume form $d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.
conclusions: the area element $d A$ is really nothing more than the standard volume form $d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$

nodes.name: Integral of a function on a surface
nodes.statement: For instance, to integrate a function $\phi: M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we would write $$ \int_{\Omega} \phi \omega=\int_{\Omega} \phi \sqrt{\operatorname{det}(g)} d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2} . $$

nodes.name: Integration under a conformal parameterization
nodes.statement: In the case of a conformal parameterization things become even simpler-since $\sqrt{\operatorname{det}(g)}=a$ we have just $$ \int_{\Omega} \phi a d x^{1} \wedge d x^{2}, $$ where $a: M \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is the scaling factor.

nodes.name: Stokes' theorem
nodes.statement: Without further ado, Stokes' theorem says that $$ \int_{\Omega} d \alpha=\int_{\partial \Omega} \alpha, $$ where $\alpha$ is any $n-1$-form on an $n$-dimensional domain $\Omega$.
also_stated_at: Remember that Stokes' theorem says $$ \int_{\Omega} d \alpha=\int_{\partial \Omega} \alpha, $$ for any $k$-form $\alpha$ and $k+1$-dimensional domain $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Divergence theorem
nodes.statement: Let's start with the divergence theorem from vector calculus, which says that $$ \int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot X d A=\int_{\partial \Omega} n \cdot X d \ell $$ where $X$ is a vector field on $\Omega$ and $n$ represents the unit normal field along the boundary of $\Omega$.
assumptions: $n$ represents the unit normal field along the boundary of $\Omega$
conclusions:
$$
\int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot X d A=\int_{\partial \Omega} n \cdot X d \ell
$$

nodes.name: Divergence theorem as a special case of Stokes
nodes.statement: Let's try writing this theorem using exterior calculus. First, remember that we can write the divergence of $X$ as $\nabla \cdot X=\star d \star X^{b}$. It's a bit harder to see how to write the right-hand side of the divergence theorem, but think about what integration does here: it takes tangents to the boundary and sticks them into a 1-form. For instance, $\int_{\partial \Omega} X^{b}$ "adds up" the tangential components of $X$. To get the normal component we could rotate $X^{p}$ by a quarter turn, which conveniently enough is achieved by hitting it with the Hodge star. Overall we get $$ \int_{\Omega} d \star X^{b}=\int_{\partial \Omega} \star X^{b}, $$ which, as promised, is just a special case of Stokes' theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite div as ★d★X♭ and the boundary flux as the integral of ★X♭; the identity is then Stokes' theorem.

nodes.name: Recall divergence in exterior calculus
nodes.statement: Let's try writing this theorem using exterior calculus. First, remember that we can write the divergence of $X$ as $\nabla \cdot X=\star d \star X^{b}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall divergence in exterior calculus

nodes.name: Normal flux via the Hodge star
nodes.statement: It's a bit harder to see how to write the right-hand side of the divergence theorem, but think about what integration does here: it takes tangents to the boundary and sticks them into a 1-form. For instance, $\int_{\partial \Omega} X^{b}$ "adds up" the tangential components of $X$. To get the normal component we could rotate $X^{p}$ by a quarter turn, which conveniently enough is achieved by hitting it with the Hodge star.
nodes.statement_short: Normal flux via the Hodge star

nodes.name: Recognize Stokes' theorem
nodes.statement: Overall we get $$ \int_{\Omega} d \star X^{b}=\int_{\partial \Omega} \star X^{b}, $$ which, as promised, is just a special case of Stokes' theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Recognize Stokes' theorem

nodes.name: Divergence as boundary flux
nodes.statement: Alternatively, we can use Stokes' theorem to provide a more geometric interpretation of the divergence operator itself: when integrated over any region $\Omega$-no matter how small-the divergence operator gives the total flux through the region boundary. In the discrete case we'll see that this boundary flux interpretation is the only notion of divergence-in other words, there's no concept of divergence at a single point.

nodes.name: Exercise 4.2 (Green's theorem)
nodes.statement: Exercise 4.2\\ Show that Stokes' theorem also implies Green's theorem, which says that $$ \int_{\Omega} \nabla \times X d A=\int_{\partial \Omega} t \cdot X d \ell $$ where $\Omega$ is a region in the plane and $t$ is a continuous unit vector field tangent to its boundary $\partial \Omega$.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
nodes.statement: It basically says that for a real-valued function $\phi: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ on the real line $$ \int_{a}^{b} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} d x=\phi(b)-\phi(a) . $$
assumptions: a real-valued function $\phi: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ on the real line

nodes.name: FTC as Stokes' theorem on an interval
nodes.statement: But soft, behold! All we've done is written Stokes' theorem once again: $$ \int_{[a, b]} d \phi=\int_{\partial[a, b]} \phi, $$ since the boundary of the interval $[a, b]$ consists only of the two endpoints $a$ and $b$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Stokes' theorem to the interval [a,b], whose boundary is its two endpoints.

nodes.name: Discrete exterior calculus (DEC)
nodes.statement: Instead, we need to keep track of a discrete (or really, finite) number of pieces of information that capture the essential behavior of the objects we're working with; we call this scheme discrete exterior calculus (or DEC for short).

nodes.name: Discrete 1-form value $\hat\alpha_e$
nodes.statement: In other words, if $\alpha$ is a 1-form and $e$ is an edge, then we'll associate the number $$ \hat{\alpha}_{e}:=\int_{e} \alpha $$ with $e$, where the (\^{}) is meant to suggest a discrete quantity (not to be confused with a unit-length vector).

nodes.name: Discrete differential $k$-form
nodes.statement: More generally, a $k$-form that has been integrated over each $k$-dimensional cell (edges in 1D, faces in 2D, etc.) is called a discrete differential $k$-form.

nodes.name: Geometric oriented $k$-simplex
nodes.statement: More generally, suppose that each element of our mesh is an oriented $k$-simplex $\sigma$, i.e., a collection of $k+1$ vertices $p_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ given in some fixed order ( $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k+1}$ ). The geometry associated with $\sigma$\\ is the convex combination of these points: $$ \left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \lambda_{i} p_{i} \mid \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \lambda_{i}=1, \lambda_{i} \geq 0\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n} $$

nodes.name: Same orientation of oriented simplices
nodes.statement: Two oriented $k$-simplices have the same orientation if and only if the vertices of one are an even permutation of the vertices of another.

nodes.name: Integrating a $k$-form over an oriented simplex
nodes.statement: Remember that a $k$-form is going to "eat" $k$ vectors at each point and spit out a number-a good canonical choice is to take the ordered collection of edge vectors $\left(p_{2}-p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k+1}-p_{1}\right)$ and orthonormalize them (using, say the Gram-Schmidt algorithm) to get vectors $\left(u_{1}, \ldots, u_{k}\right)$. This way the sign of the integrand changes whenever the orientation changes. Numerically, we can then approximate the integral via a sum $$ \int_{\sigma} \alpha \approx \frac{|\sigma|}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_{p_{i}}\left(u_{1}, \ldots, u_{k}\right) $$ where $\left\{p_{i}\right\}$ is a (usually carefully-chosen) collection of sample points.
nodes.statement_short: Orthonormalize the simplex edge vectors by Gram-Schmidt, then average the form on them over sample points and scale by the simplex volume.

nodes.name: Orthonormalize the edge vectors
nodes.statement: Remember that a $k$-form is going to "eat" $k$ vectors at each point and spit out a number-a good canonical choice is to take the ordered collection of edge vectors $\left(p_{2}-p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k+1}-p_{1}\right)$ and orthonormalize them (using, say the Gram-Schmidt algorithm) to get vectors $\left(u_{1}, \ldots, u_{k}\right)$. This way the sign of the integrand changes whenever the orientation changes.
nodes.statement_short: Orthonormalize the edge vectors

nodes.name: Approximate the integral by a sample sum
nodes.statement: Numerically, we can then approximate the integral via a sum $$ \int_{\sigma} \alpha \approx \frac{|\sigma|}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_{p_{i}}\left(u_{1}, \ldots, u_{k}\right) $$ where $\left\{p_{i}\right\}$ is a (usually carefully-chosen) collection of sample points.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the integral by a sample sum

nodes.name: Discrete 0-form
nodes.statement: Well, it must be a 0-form (i.e., a function) that's been integrated over every 0 -simplex $v_{i}$ (i.e., vertex) of a mesh: $$ \hat{\phi}_{i}=\int_{v_{i}} \phi $$ By convention, the integral of a function over a zero-dimensional set is simply the value of the function at that point: $\hat{\phi}_{i}=\phi\left(v_{i}\right)$.

nodes.name: Discrete exterior derivative on a triangle
nodes.statement: For instance, if $\hat{\alpha}$ is a discrete 1-form stored on the three edges of a triangle $\sigma$, then we have $$ \int_{\sigma} d \alpha=\int_{\partial \sigma} \alpha=\sum_{i=1}^{3} \int_{e_{i}} \alpha=\sum_{i=1}^{3} \hat{\alpha}_{i} . $$ \begin{center} \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}]{5ca462c8-87f1-4b78-bcfe-c2b572a4db96-58_252_241_2000_942} \end{center} In other words, we can exactly evaluate the integral on the left by just adding up three numbers. Pretty cool!

nodes.name: Discrete exterior derivative
nodes.statement: In fact, the thing on the left is also a discrete differential form: it's the 2-form $d \alpha$ integrated over the only triangle in our mesh. So for convenience, we'll call this guy " $\hat{d} \hat{\alpha}^{\prime}$ ", and we'll call the operation $\hat{d}$ the discrete exterior derivative. (In the future we will drop the hats from our\\ notation when the meaning is clear from context.) In other words, the discrete exterior derivative takes a $k$-form that has already been integrated over each $k$-simplex and applies Stokes' theorem to get the integral of the derivative over each $k+1$-simplex.
nodes.statement_short: d-hat sums a discrete k-form over the boundary of each (k+1)-simplex, i.e. applies Stokes' theorem cellwise.

nodes.name: Discrete exterior derivative with signs
nodes.statement: For instance, in the example below we'd have $$ (\hat{d} \hat{\alpha})_{1}=\hat{\alpha}_{1}+\hat{\alpha}_{2}+\hat{\alpha}_{3} $$ and $$ (\hat{d} \hat{\alpha})_{2}=\hat{\alpha}_{4}+\hat{\alpha}_{5}-\hat{\alpha}_{2} . $$

nodes.name: Dual mesh
nodes.statement: In general, the dual of an $n$-dimensional simplicial mesh identifies every $k$-simplex in the primal (i.e., original) mesh with a unique $(n-k)$-cell in the dual mesh.

nodes.name: Orthogonal dual
nodes.statement: A dual mesh is an orthogonal dual if primal and dual elements are contained in orthogonal linear subspaces. For\\ instance, on a planar triangle mesh a dual edge would make a right angle with the corresponding primal edge. For curved domains, we ask only that primal and dual elements be orthogonal intrinsically, e.g., if one rigidly unfolds a pair of neighboring triangles into the plane, the primal and dual edges should again be orthogonal.
differentia: primal and dual elements are contained in orthogonal linear subspaces

nodes.name: Discrete Hodge dual
nodes.statement: In particular, the discrete Hodge dual of a (discrete) $k$-form on the primal mesh is an ( $n-k$ )-form on the dual mesh. Similarly, the Hodge dual of an $k$-form on the dual mesh is an ( $n-k$ )-form on the primal mesh.

nodes.name: Primal and dual forms
nodes.statement: Discrete forms on the primal mesh are called primal forms and discrete forms on the dual mesh are called dual forms.

nodes.name: Notation $\hat\star\hat\alpha$
nodes.statement: Given a discrete form $\hat{\alpha}$ (whether primal or dual), we'll write its Hodge dual as $\hat{\star} \hat{\alpha}$.

nodes.name: Primal and dual forms live in different places
nodes.statement: Unlike continuous forms, discrete primal and dual forms live in different places (so for instance, discrete primal $k$-forms and dual $k$-forms cannot be added to each other). In fact, primal and dual forms often have different physical interpretations. For instance, a primal 1-form might represent the total circulation along edges of the primal mesh, whereas in the same context a dual 1-form might represent the total flux through the corresponding dual edges (see illustration above).

nodes.name: Diagonal Hodge star
nodes.statement: Consider a primal $k$-form $\alpha$. If $\hat{\alpha}_{i}$ is the value of $\hat{\alpha}$ on the $k$-simplex $\sigma_{i}$, then the diagonal Hodge star is defined by $$ \hat{\star} \hat{\alpha}_{i}=\frac{\left|\sigma_{i}^{\star}\right|}{\left|\sigma_{i}\right|} \hat{\alpha}_{i} $$ for all $i$, where $|\sigma|$ indicates the (unsigned) volume of $\sigma$ (which by convention equals one for a vertex!) and $\left|\sigma^{\star}\right|$ is the volume of the corresponding dual cell.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal Hodge star: scale each primal value by the ratio of dual-cell to primal-cell volume.

nodes.name: Dual Hodge star inverts primal Hodge star
nodes.statement: It's not hard to see, then, that Hodge star taking dual forms to primal forms (the dual Hodge star) is the inverse of the one that takes primal to dual (the primal Hodge star).
conclusions: Hodge star taking dual forms to primal forms (the dual Hodge star) is the inverse of the one that takes primal to dual (the primal Hodge star)

nodes.name: Complete discrete exterior calculus
nodes.statement: Coming up with a complete discrete calculus where the whole cast of characters $d, \wedge, \star, \mathcal{L}_{X}, i_{\alpha}$, etc., plays well together is an active and ongoing area of research.
